newsitem.title: UK: GE aeroengines sees profits accelerating.
newsitem.headline: GE aeroengines sees profits accelerating.

text.p: The president of General Electric (GE) Aircraft Engines, Gene Murphy, said he expected solid profit growth to the end of the decade.
Operating profits should rise to over 20 percent of revenue in 1996, Murphy said, after their recovery in 1995 back to 19 percent following a steady decline in the early 1990s.

"It should be over 20 percent this year," he told Reuters at the Farnborough air show, adding that the fundamental strengthening of underlying civil and defence aircraft markets should make it possible to keep margins over 20 percent for the next five years or so.
"What happens after 2002 or so, I don't think anyone would want to predict", he said.
Murphy said the company and its French partner Snecma were in what he described as "a defining year" for the General Electric Corp unit.
Behind the upturn lay "a long-awaited recovery in the commercial sector and a return to profitability for airlines", he told a news conference.

In the newly-active marketplace, however, there were also greater demands on suppliers, he said, which made the company's continuing eforts to improve both manufacturing and internal corporate processes important to keep costs in check.
One example of the kind of customer-driven work underway was an ongoing study to prepare an engine solution for Airbus Industrie's proposed stretch A340-600.

Murphy said the latest indications from this study phase, due to be completed later this year, were that GE would be offering a completely new engine for the plane rather than a derivative of its existing CF6 engine.

"If the A340-600 goes forward we would certainly welcome Snecma's participation in that aircraft," he added, even though the thrust demands for the four-engined passenger aircraft, at about 56,000 pounds per unit, was outside the current range of power covered by the two companies' teaming arrangement.
Separately from its engine sales, GE has high ambitions for increasing its annual turnover from services, including maintenance and spares, by some 50 percent to $3.0 billion from $2.0 billion.
Murphy said the company was seeking double-digit annual turnover growth in the coming years, partly on the back of the organic growth in spares sales that should track its rising engine sales.

At a time when engine orders remained tightly-priced and left fairly narrow profit margins, the engine services activities offered higher margins, lower investment costs and were generally more cash generative than engine making, he said.
